nameStory: The martagon lily gets its name from the Turkish word 'turban,' referring to how its swept-back petals resemble a Turkish cap or turban when fully opened. It's also called Turk's cap lily for this same reason, though this nickname can cause confusion since we have a native Turk's cap lily right here in New England!
description: The martagon lily is a tall, elegant European lily that occasionally shows up in New England gardens and naturalized areas. Growing 3-6 feet tall, it produces distinctive nodding flowers with strongly recurved petals that curve backward like a turban. The flowers are typically pink to purplish with darker spots, and they dangle gracefully from the top portion of the stem. This is primarily a garden escape rather than a truly wild plant in our region.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Distinctive nodding flowers with petals that curve dramatically backward, creating a turban-like shape; usually pink to purplish with dark purple spots throughout

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves arranged in whorls (circles) around the stem at regular intervals, with a smooth, waxy texture that feels firm to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, straight stem reaching 3-6 feet with flowers clustered in the upper portion, each flower dangling from its own curved stalk

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Upright seed capsules that split open to reveal flat, papery seeds stacked like coins inside three chambers

habitat: Extremely rare in New England, with only one recorded observation, likely from an old garden escape or naturalized population. When found, it typically grows in rich, well-drained woodland edges or abandoned garden sites with partial shade. Prefers cool, moist conditions similar to those found in European mountain meadows.

seasonality.spring: Shoots emerge early with distinctive whorled leaves already visible, growing rapidly through late spring.
seasonality.summer: Blooms in early to mid-summer with the characteristic nodding, recurved flowers that emit a sweet, somewhat musky fragrance.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and split open, while leaves begin to yellow and die back to the underground bulb.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground parts visible, surviving as a deep bulb beneath the soil.

funFact: This lily is so adapted to cool climates that its bulbs actually require a cold winter period to bloom properly - they simply won't flower in warm southern regions, no matter how well you care for them!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with our native Turk's cap lily, but the martagon lily has whorled leaves (arranged in circles around the stem) while Turk's cap lily has alternate leaves. Remember: martagon has 'married' leaves that cluster together in whorls.
contextualKnowledge: The naming confusion between martagon lily and Turk's cap lily creates real identification challenges - both are called 'Turk's cap lily' in different sources. When reading about lilies, always check the scientific name to know which species is being discussed.
compareHints: Unlike our native lilies, martagon lily has distinctly whorled leaves rather than alternate or scattered leaf arrangements. The recurved petals are more dramatically swept back than even our native Turk's cap lily, and the flower color tends toward pink-purple rather than the orange-red typical of most native New England lilies.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's true lilies, Canada lily is the only one with consistently downward-facing, bell-shaped flowers in yellow to orange shades.
Unlike its relatives Canada lily and Turk's-cap lily which have downward-facing or nodding flowers, wood lily is the only native lily in New England that consistently faces its flowers upward.
Among New England's lilies, tiger lily is the only one with black bulbils in the leaf joints and the only non-native species commonly encountered.

Among New England's native lilies, Turk's-cap lily is the tallest and most dramatic, with its hanging orange flowers and completely recurved petals setting it apart from the upward-facing Canada lily and the smaller, red Wood lily.
Among New England's true lilies, Michigan lily is distinguished by its moderate height (shorter than Turk's-cap lily but taller than wood lily) and its orange color with backward-curved petals.
Unlike our native Canada lily and Turk's-cap lily which have drooping, downward-facing flowers, Formosa lily blooms face outward horizontally.
